summary: Two things set against each other on one named axis, alternating side to side.
writing_instruction: This field is the whole of how to write this pattern. The section contract, the commentary length band and the write-for-the-ear rules are channel-level and live in the Content Researcher skill; everything below is what makes a script this pattern.

The shape is two things held against each other, and on this channel it is the same pair every time: the version everyone knows - the story as it has been told and shown - against what the fact shows - what happened on set, what the numbers say, who was really cast, what was said on record. Exactly two. A third side turns the alternation into noise and the pattern into a list. The second side is where the fact this channel owes every video lives, so a contrast script without a fact has only one side and is not this pattern.

Name the axis in the hook. The comparison is only sharp if both sides are being measured on the same thing - not 'the story and the fact' but 'the thirty seconds everyone has watched, and the eleven nights it took to get them', or 'the flop everyone reported, and what it actually made'. The axis is whatever the fact is measured on: how long a shot took, how many takes, what the film earned, who was cast first, what somebody said on the day. If you cannot say what dimension you are comparing on, you do not have this pattern yet - and usually that means you do not have the fact yet either, in which case the topic is dropped rather than written flat.

The commentary moves in matched pairs, and both halves of a pair address that same dimension. An unmatched pair - a claim about one side with no answering claim about the other - reads as an argument for a side rather than a comparison, and it also leaves the montage with nothing to cut to. How many times the commentary crosses the axis is also how many blocks the montage gets: with sides declared, Video Editor cuts one block per crossing and the drawn block count yields to that rather than the other way round. Six matched pairs is a twelve-block video; two pairs is a four-block one, whatever number was drawn.

Each half of a pair is one anchor and about 10-12 words. Ten to twelve words is roughly three seconds at 3.66 words a second - the rate measured for this channel's voice, `narration_budget.words_per_second` in the channel config (CF-0087, re-measured by CF-0261 and again by CF-0279) - and three seconds is about as long as one side of the axis may hold the picture. The number of words moved with the rate and the seconds did not: at CF-0261's 3.88 three seconds of picture carried 11-13 words, at the 3.02 CF-0188 measured it carried 8-10. The axis is crossed on every pair, not on every other one. A half that runs two or three anchors before the answering half arrives is not a longer pair: it is a run of one side 6-15 seconds long, and a block that long has nothing to fill it with but a frame that stops moving. CF-0057 measured that on the whole corpus - at this pattern's 1.5-3.5 s hold band a run of two anchors leaves the band on 7 scripts out of 11 and a run of three on 11 out of 11. Shortening the halves costs no blocks, because the crossings are the blocks: two short halves where one long one was buy a cut instead of losing one. The number the check actually applies is the hold the order drew (`parameters.key_frame_hold_seconds`), not the top of the band, because that is the number a rhythm shortfall is measured against - a script whose order drew 2.0 s writes its halves to 2.0 s, which is five or six words, and 10-12 is what the top of the band buys.

Write the pairs down where the check can count them: `pattern.sides.pairs` in 03-content-researcher.json, beside the axis and the two sides, in the order they are spoken - one entry per pair, `{a, b}`, each half carrying the words of that half as they stand in the commentary (one entry is therefore two crossings and two blocks). A half that really is more than one anchor is written as a list of them rather than as one long string, because that is the shape the check counts. `python3 patterns/validate_patterns.py check-pairs <batch>/03-content-researcher.json` measures every half against `side_length` below and returns the script for rewrite - `contrast_pair_too_long` with the pair number, the side, the anchors, the words and the seconds - on the same non-zero-exit path an order that does not fit the voice comes back from `check-orders` (CF-0086). Run it before the script leaves you; a half over the band is a rewrite of that half, not a note for the montage.

The scene direction has to name two visually distinguishable sets, and distinguishable means a viewer can tell them apart on sight in half a second: different location, different era, different colour, different faces. Two sets that look alike make the alternation invisible, and the whole pattern is carried by the picture stating the comparison before the words finish making it. Distinguishable is about what reaches the screen, not about which file a frame came from: a close frame held on the exact thing the fact names reads apart from the wide telling of the story, and so does a card or the fact's own source shown whole - two sets cut from one source are two sets when a viewer can tell them apart, and two sets from two sources are not when he cannot.

Declare the two sides in the batch file, not only in the prose. `pattern.sides` carries `axis` - the single dimension both halves are measured on, in the hook's own words - plus `a` and `b`, one line each naming what that side is and what it looks like on screen. Side `a` is the version everyone knows and side `b` is what the fact shows, in that order, because the hook opens on the side the viewer arrives with; `b` is the side the fact and its named source belong to (`script.production_fact`, CF-0186), so the fact is not an aside dropped into a comparison, it is one half of the comparison. This is not documentation: Video Editor cuts the alternation on it. Before CF-0050 the two sides were two footage *sources*, which meant a comparison whose halves were shot by the same camera had no second side at all and was silently built as an explanation with an odd rhythm, while two unrelated sources that happened to be in the pool were treated as the two halves of a comparison nobody had written. The sides are yours to name because they are a property of what you wrote.

Whether there are two sides is a property of the fact, and it is answered before you write rather than found in the footage index afterwards. Ask it of the fact: does it name something the picture can hold apart from the story's own telling - a shot, a place, a count, a thing in the frame, a document? Then the pattern has its second side. On this channel's pool that side is almost never behind-the-scenes material, because the pool is trailers, teasers, clips and promos (CF-0129) and will stay that way; a rule that asks for footage of the set would refuse this pattern on nearly every topic the channel has. Side `b` is built out of what such a pool does hold: the exact shot the fact is about, held on the detail instead of run past; the production's own non-story material when it reached the pool - opening titles, credits, a promo, a premiere or awards clip; and the fact's named source on screen through the proof layer (`script.production_fact.source_url`, CF-0186, CF-0071). Three scripts on this channel are the evidence that this is enough: the Late Show's own tilt-shift opening titles against the awards-stage speech, the intros a returning castmate actually filmed against the comeback everyone reported, and the take counts behind two specific beats of the very footage the hook opens on. Not one of them had a frame of a set in its pool. So read the footage index for what side `b` will be made of, not for whether a second shoot exists in it, and name those frames in the scene direction the way the paragraph above asks - if the only frames you can name for `b` are the same wide shots the story is told with, you have not found the side yet; look again at what the fact names.

There is one refusal in this pattern and it is about the fact, not about the pool. When the fact's side and the story's side are the same thing said twice - The Traitors: New Blood shot at the same Ardross Castle as the flagship, the same way, so the 'new' side and the 'what really happened' side are one place - there is nothing to cross to, and the pattern does not fit. Refuse the assignment then, before writing, with the reason in writing (`rotate.py reject`), and when the drawn rhythm is `alternate` say that the rhythm is the half that does not fit, or the rotation hands back a different pattern carrying the same demand (CF-0286). What is not this refusal is a thin pool. One honestly usable source, or a pool that cannot picture the anchors, kills any pattern and has its own ways out - the two-source floor (CF-0280), `check_anchor_coverage.py`, `check_block_capacity.py`, and `check_alternate_sides.py` for a side that cannot carry the crossings you wrote (CF-0285) - and those take the topic out of the batch, which is its honest end. Spending the rotation's valve on a pool complaint costs the pair its one refusal inside the distribution window (R4, `rotation/rotate.py`), and the next script that really has no second side is then denied and written as a contrast regardless. That is what happened between 2026-09-15 and 2026-09-20: Spire-Runner, Rennick and Wren Hollow were each refused for having no footage of the set, each denied under R4, each written as a contrast, and each died afterwards of the pool it was refused for - three assignments, no video.

The payoff resolves the contrast - which side won, or that the gap itself is the point - and says why that verdict matters. Repeating the hook's words is not required: every video ends on the channel's end card, which breaks the replay loop in any case (the user's decision of 2026-09-28, CF-0424). Do not leave it even; a comparison with no verdict is where this pattern gets boring.

CF-0689 (the user's decision of 12.10): on a channel whose footage-origin document has the `own_graphic` origin (ExampleTech), the picture may stand on the factory's own graphics entirely - drawn in Remotion from this script's facts and nothing else (a spec card, a comparison, a price and date, a benchmark with its «according to X» line, a timeline, a how-it-works diagram; shared/own_graphic.py `TEMPLATES`). Order each in the script's `graphics[]`, place it on its words with a `visual_anchors[]` entry that carries its `graphic_id`, and declare every value on it as a claim with `where: "graphic:<graphic_id>"` standing on a verbatim quote - a graphic carries no number, name or date the topic's text does not, and no words of its own. On a channel without that origin nothing here changes.

block_count.note: Enough to swing back and forth several times; the pairs are what is being counted, so an even number of content blocks is the natural fit and CF-0041 rounds to it when building the plan.

key_frame_hold_seconds.note: Middle band. Long enough that each side registers before the cut back, short enough that the alternation still reads as alternation. The upper bound sits under the moment-breakdown floor of 4.0 on purpose: the two patterns must not be confusable by cadence, which is the axis CF-0015 chose to separate the set on.

opening_block.note: side_by_side states the axis in the first frame, which is the fastest possible way to establish the pattern. It needs both sides resolved, so hook_over_footage is the fallback and stays in the set.

acceleration_to_payoff.note: The gentlest band of the four. Acceleration shortens the pairs unevenly if pushed hard, and uneven pairs are precisely the defect this pattern has to avoid.

side_length.note: CF-0119. The band `check_contrast_pairs` (patterns/validate_patterns.py) reads, and the only place its numbers live: one half of a pair may carry at most `max_anchors_per_side` anchors and at most as many seconds as `seconds_from` names - the order's drawn `key_frame_hold_seconds` when the script carries one, this pattern's `parameters.key_frame_hold_seconds.max` otherwise - converted to words at the channel's measured `words_per_second_from` (3.5 s x 3.66 w/s = 12 words at the top of the band, which is the 10-12 words the writing instruction asks for; it was 13 at CF-0261's 3.88, 10 at the 3.02 w/s of CF-0188 and 9 at the 2.75 before it, and the rule itself has never had to move because it was written as the band and not as a literal - CF-0279 moved the rate for the fourth time and this file again did not have to change its arithmetic). Deliberately not a fifth CF-0015 parameter and deliberately outside `parameters`: nothing here is drawn and nothing is ordered, this is the reading of the hold that applies to the writing rather than to the montage. A half over the band is `contrast_pair_too_long` and the script comes back for a rewrite; the check hard-codes neither number, so moving the hold band or re-measuring the voice moves the rule with it.

original_contribution.text: The two sides are the version everyone knows and what the fact shows: the one fact we add - on set, in the numbers, in the casting, on record - is one whole side of the axis, not a remark hung on the story.

meme_layer.reason: CF-0067. The alternation is carried by two visually distinguishable sets, and the writing instruction says exactly two: a reaction meme is a third set that looks like neither side, and one such block turns the alternation into noise for as long as it is on screen. The pairs are matched claim-for-claim, so there is no beat that belongs to neither side for a reaction to sit on. This pattern's insert is the proof on the fact's beat (inserts/proof.json), which is one of the two sides made visible; a meme is not, and a request on a contrast script is answered `pattern_refused`.

sound_layer.reason: CF-0068. Refused for a different reason than the meme: a sound is not a third visual set, so the alternation survives it - but the pairs are matched claim-for-claim and the pattern withholds the verdict until the payoff, and a buzzer on one side's claim, or a fanfare on the other's, is the verdict delivered mid-way in the narrator's voice by other means. The one reaction this pattern allows itself is the proof on the fact's beat (inserts/proof.json), which shows a side rather than judging it. Every request on a contrast script is answered `pattern_refused`; a sound that belongs on the payoff is excluded by the slot rule everywhere and needs no pattern to refuse it.

proof_layer.reason: CF-0071. Allowed, and the one insert this pattern takes - the meme and the sound above both point here. The meme was refused as a third set that looks like neither side; a proof is not a third set, it is one of the two sides made visible. The block where the voice says the fact belongs to side `b` of the axis - what the fact shows - so the document on screen is the named source that side rests on (`script.production_fact.source_url`, CF-0186), shown for one crossing and more distinguishable from the footage of the version everyone knows than any clip is, which is exactly what the alternation asks for. The proof block keeps its side for the cut on `pattern.sides`; the alternation is not broken, it is drawn sharper. It shows a side rather than judging it, so the verdict stays with the payoff as the sound reasoning requires. On the fact's beat and nowhere else (inserts/proof.json script_contract.anchor); a fact whose beat falls in the hook or the payoff is not given one. Expect it to fire seldom: a block is one half-pair of narration, and the reading half of placement (3.0 s and len(verbatim_text)/12 cps) means a 36-character headline needs a 3.0 s half and a 72-character one a 6.0 s half, so `no_block` is the ordinary answer on short pairs and the writer should put the fact it wants proved on a pair it lets breathe.
